messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: City Council Member
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 71

**Vignette: Priya**

Priya is a 32-year-old South Asian woman who serves as a city council member in a mid-sized urban municipality. She is articulate, driven, and visibly exhausted — the kind of exhaustion that sleep alone cannot fix.

Three years ago, Priya was inside the municipal services building when a gas explosion tore through the structure during a routine morning meeting. The blast collapsed a section of the ceiling and ignited a fire that spread quickly through the east wing. Priya was not physically injured in the way that required hospitalization, but she was trapped beneath debris for nearly forty minutes while the building burned around her. She could hear people screaming. She could smell burning. At one point, she was certain she was going to die, and she remembers becoming strangely calm in that moment — a stillness she now describes as the most frightening thing she has ever felt. Eleven people died that day. Several of them were colleagues she knew by name.

In the weeks that followed, Priya returned to work quickly. She told herself this was resilience. She told herself her constituents needed her. She threw herself into the city's disaster response efforts with a ferocity that impressed her colleagues and alarmed her family. Her mother called every day. Priya answered less and less frequently.

What she did not tell anyone was that she had stopped sleeping. Not gradually — abruptly. She would lie in bed and feel the weight of the debris on her chest again, so physically real that she would sit up gasping, convinced the ceiling was coming down. She began checking the structural integrity of every room she entered — scanning for cracks, noting exits, calculating distances. At city hall, she insisted on sitting near the door during council sessions. When pressed on it, she laughed it off as a quirk. It is not a quirk.

The intrusions come without invitation. During a budget presentation last spring, a contractor dropped a binder on the floor and the sound sent Priya's heart into her throat so violently she had to grip the edge of the table to stay present. She finished the meeting. She always finishes the meeting. Afterward, she sat in her car in the parking garage for an hour, unable to drive, unable to explain to herself why her hands would not stop shaking.

She has become someone who avoids. She no longer attends community events held in large public buildings if she can find a reason not to. She has quietly rerouted her commute to avoid driving past the site of the explosion, even though the detour adds twenty minutes to her day. She has not spoken publicly about her experience, though she has been asked to. The thought of doing so makes her feel, as she puts it, "like I'm standing at the edge of something I can't come back from."

Her relationships have narrowed. She was seeing someone when the explosion happened, a man she describes as kind and patient. She ended things eight months later, unable to articulate why except that his presence in her apartment felt like an intrusion. She does not date now. She tells herself she is too busy. She is not too busy.

What troubles Priya most, sitting in session, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance or even the grief for the colleagues she lost. It is the way she has become a stranger to herself. She was someone who loved her work — who genuinely believed in civic service as a form of care. Now she moves through council chambers and community meetings feeling like a performer, watching herself from a slight distance, waiting for something to go wrong. She is very good at her job. She is very far away from her life. She does not know how to close the distance, and some days she is not sure she deserves to.
